messages.content: You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery (0A+0B)
Accepted scope: Launch and deep-space delivery of all Phase 0 hardware to its operating location; LEO price and delivered price kept separate.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- add · Earth-to-space launch/delivery · supported by all · quantity: Claude 2.5–6 kt; Gemini 2.5–3.5 kt; GPT 2.5–8 kt · cost: Claude $3–15B total; Gemini $3–6B total; GPT $3,000–12,000/kg · confidence: low

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-8: Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery (0A + 0B)

**Project Dyson, Phase 0 (revised architecture). Proposal Rev A, for the configuration-controlled baseline.**
All costs are in constant 2026 USD. Masses are metric tonnes (t) and kilotonnes (kt).

---

## 0. Position in One Page

1. **Launch high, never spiral.** Every Phase 0 element leaves Earth on a direct high-energy trajectory, a low-energy transfer to SEL1 at C3 ≈ −0.7 km²/s². I reject LEO aggregation followed by an electric-propulsion (EP) spiral as the baseline. MW-class arrays would loiter for months in the most congested debris band and would take Van Allen belt dose. Under the ALARP debris posture (D-03), that is hard to justify.

2. **SEL1 is the single delivery gateway.** The Phase 1 receiving node (bom-0-13) is already at SEL1. Everything Earth-launched is handed over there. The MW tugs (bom-0-4) carry site hardware, spares and site propellant to the NEA on their outbound legs, which would otherwise fly empty. The heliocentric leg is therefore a marginal cost, not a separate delivery fleet.

3. **One module standard, dual-sourced.** All hardware is designed as "Class M" modules: ≤12.0 t separated mass at C3 = −0.7, inside a Ø4.5 m × 10 m envelope. That fits at least two vendors' rockets. Super-heavy vehicles (Class H) are a bundling upside, not a design dependency. This has a direct consequence for bom-0-4: **tugs should launch as at most two modules of ≤12 t each, which points to roughly 1.2–1.5 MWe per tug.** The 2.5 MWe top of the round-2 range does not survive this constraint unless refuelled super-heavy delivery to C3 ≈ 0 is demonstrated before KDP-0B.

4. **Propellant is most of the mass, so it is a separate sub-line.** Earth-launched EP propellant is 50–65% of the launched mass in the central case. It scales with 0B throughput × duration. Hardware mass is nearly fixed. Carrying them as one number hides the decision the 0B gate actually has to make.

5. **The numbers:**
   - **Launched mass:** 2.4 kt central, 1.3–4.5 kt P10–P90.
   - **Cost:** 0A ≈ $0.42B firm request. 0B ≈ $9.3B P50 (P10–P90 $4–16B) as a planning value, re-sized at the gate.

6. **Earth-supply benchmark (my most important finding).** This line also supplies the price model for the Earth-supplied-material fallback. Phase 0 pays a "launch tax" of about 30–45% of the benchmark price on every kilogram of product, regardless of launch price. As launch gets cheaper, the non-launch costs of 0B do not fall, so 0B's relative economics get *worse*. The economic gate at KDP-0B must use the same price model on both sides.

---

## 1. Scope and Boundaries

### 1.1 What bom-0-8 owns

| Sub-line | Content |
|---|---|
| **8a Hardware delivery** | Launch services for every Phase 0 hardware element. Payload adapters and dispensers. Passive-cargo pallets. Integration, mission assurance, launch-site campaign services. Delivery to SEL1 handover, or to C3 hand-off for self-propelled scouts and the pathfinder. |
| **8b Propellant delivery** | Launch of sealed EP propellant cartridges. The Earth Departure Carrier (EDC) bus that takes them to SEL1 handover. |
| **8c Delivery infrastructure** | Leased integration facility and iodine handling cell. Launch-campaign management. Launch-price indexing. Delivery ICD control. |

### 1.2 What bom-0-8 does not own

| Item | Owner |
|---|---|
| Propellant commodity, supply audit, cartridge manufacture and filling | bom-0-16 |
| Tug hardware, tug operations, outbound-leg propellant consumption | bom-0-4, bom-0-10, bom-0-16 |
| Ground stations and DSN-equivalent time for EDC tracking | bom-0-9 |
| Launch-loss reserve | bom-0-17 (recommended value given in §11) |
| Disposal policy | bom-0-15 (bom-0-8 implements it for upper stages and EDCs) |
| Earth-supplied-material fallback | Phase 1 cost. bom-0-8 supplies only the price model. |

### 1.3 Handover definition

"Delivered" for 8a and 8b means: the item is in the SEL1 operations volume, a halo of A_z ≈ 300,000–700,000 km, outside the solar exclusion zone. It is also passivated or held by the receiving node or a tug, and its health has been checked. After handover, bom-0-4 owns the "delivered at operating location" leg.

Three prices are always reported separately:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P_LEO** | Price per kg to low Earth orbit (reference only; not used for Phase 0 delivery) |
| **P_dep** | Launch-service price per kg at Earth departure, C3 = −0.7 |
| **P_hand** | Fully burdened price per kg at SEL1 handover |
| **P_site** | Price per kg at the NEA site. Reported as a memo with bom-0-4/0-16 allocations shown, not double-counted. |

---

## 2. Design Philosophy

| # | Principle | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Launch high; no LEO loitering of large structures | Direct injection to SEL1 transfer. LEO-depot routes stay study-only. |
| P2 | Design to the second-best launcher | Class M = 12 t at C3 −0.7. Super-heavy capacity is used by bundling, never assumed. |
| P3 | Outbound tug legs are free capacity | No dedicated deep-space delivery fleet. Site cargo is staged at SEL1. |
| P4 | Risk-tier the manifest | Propellant (fungible, loss-tolerant) flies on new or discounted vehicles. Unique critical hardware flies on mature vehicles. |
| P5 | No single launch failure removes more than one-third of any critical function | Drives module splits for the plant and power (Requirement DEL-006). |
| P6 | Self-insure through spares and functional redundancy | No commercial insurance; premiums are 8–12%. A loss reserve is held in bom-0-17. |
| P7 | Swap containers, don't transfer fluids | Iodine moves as sealed cartridges that mate mechanically, avoiding in-space solid or vapour transfer. |
| P8 | Price symmetry | The same P_dep model is used for Phase 0 cost and for the Earth-supply benchmark. |

---

## 3. System Architecture

### 3.1 Flow

```
                    EARTH  (integration facility + iodine handling cell, Florida)
                      |
      +---------------+----------------+--------------------+
      | Class S              | Class M (≤12 t)        | Class H (bundle 6–8 M)
      | ESPA-Grande rideshare| FH / Vulcan / NG+kick  | refuelled super-heavy
      | scouts 200–600 kg    | / Starship expendable  | (upside, not baseline)
      v                      v                        v
   C3 ≈ −0.7…+2       DIRECT INJECTION, C3 ≈ −0.7 km²/s²  (belts crossed in hours)
   (self-propelled      upper stage → heliocentric disposal (LGA-biased) or Earth reentry
    EP scouts →                 |
    NEA targets)                v   90–120 d low-energy transfer, TCM+insertion ≤ 50 m/s
                     +------------------------------------------+
                     |   SEL1 GATEWAY (halo, A_z 0.3–0.7 Mkm)   |
                     |   bom-0-13 receiving node                |
                     |   - parks EDC/pallets (passive targets)  |
                     |   - tugs mate cargo + I2 cartridges      |
                     +----------------+-------------------------+
                          ^           |  outbound: site hardware, spares, site I2
         Fe-Ni product    |           v  (marginal Δv cost only)
         (inbound)        |   +----------------------------+
                          +---|  MW CARGO TUGS (bom-0-4)   |
                              |  1.2–1.5 MWe recommended   |
                              +--------------+-------------+
                                             v
                                   TARGET NEA SITE (bom-0-2/3/5/6)
```

### 3.2 Delivery-mode trade

| Mode | Description | P_hand (central) | Debris / ALARP | Schedule | TRL (2026) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **D: Direct high-energy injection** | Class M to C3 −0.7, low-energy transfer to SEL1 | $3.8k–4.7k/kg | Good: belts crossed in hours; stages disposed heliocentric | 3–4 months, no window constraint | 9 (DSCOVR, SOHO, ACE heritage) | **Baseline** |
| R: Refuelled super-heavy | 80–100 t per departure, 3–6 tanker flights | $1.5k–4k/kg | Good, but many LEO flights | Fast | 5 (orbital transfer demo pending) | **Upside**; bundles Class M units |
| L: LEO aggregation + tug spiral | Tug spirals 7.7 km/s from LEO with cargo | ≈ P_LEO × 1.5 + tug time ≈ $2.5k/kg | Poor (see note) | Spiral 1–18 months, mass-dependent | 6–7 | **Rejected** for tugs |
| P: LEO depot + dedicated cislunar EP shuttle (propellant only) | Iodine to LEO, small shuttle to SEL1 | $1.8k–2.5k/kg | Moderate | Slow but continuous | 4 | **Study** until KDP-0B; could save $1–2B in the central case |
| K: Chemical kick stage from LEO | Separately launched kick stage, LEO rendezvous | ≈ P_LEO × 2.6–3 | Moderate | Fast | 6 | Inferior to D or R |

**Why Mode L is rejected:**
- A 1.5 MWe tug carries about 4,000–4,500 m² of array.
- In the 600–1,200 km band, that gives order 10⁻² expected ≥1 cm debris impacts per tug spiral. Exposure is 1.5–18 months depending on cargo.
- It also takes inner-belt dose of roughly 5–15% power loss even with 150 µm coverglass.

### 3.3 Why SEL1 suits launch (input to D-04)

- SEL1 is the cheapest Lagrange destination from Earth, at C3 ≈ −0.7. That is similar to a lunar transfer, so launcher performance tables apply directly.
- The insertion Δv on a stable manifold is near zero.
- **There is no launch window tied to NEA synodic periods.** Departures can be bought any month, which lowers price in a flexible-date market.

Moving the gateway to SEL4/L5 would push hardware C3 to roughly +1 to +3 with phasing time. That would cost launch capacity and add 1–2 years of delivery latency. This is a launch-side argument *for* D-04. It should be weighed at the 0B gate, not assumed.

---

## 4. Mass Ledger

### 4.1 Phase 0A (launches about 2028–2031)

| EP rendezvous scouts (bom-0-1) | 0.8 t | 2.4 t | 6.0 t | 4–10 × 200–600 kg; central 6 × 400 kg |

| Water pilot (bom-0-6) | 0 | 0 | 30 t | Only if a C-type target is confirmed |

### 4.3 Phase 0B propellant (8b)

The demand basis is 0.15–0.35 kg of Earth-launched iodine per kg of product delivered to SEL1:
- Round-trip SEL1↔NEA Δv of 3–6 km/s.
- Isp of 2,000–3,000 s.
- Payload of 150–300 t per trip.
- Plus the outbound hardware haul.

The final demand number belongs to bom-0-16. I use it here only to size launches.

| Case | Product | Net iodine | Gross launched (12% tare) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 0.6 kt/yr × 4 yr × 0.15 | 0.36–0.4 kt | 0.45 kt |
| Central | 1.3 kt/yr × 5 yr × 0.215 | 1.4 kt | 1.57 kt |
| High | 2.2 kt/yr × 6 yr × 0.23 (or harder Δv) | 3.0 kt | 3.36 kt |

### 4.4 Totals

| | Low corner | Central | High corner | P10–P90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Launched mass | 0.87 kt | **2.43 kt** | 5.3 kt | **1.3–4.5 kt** |

At the central case, propellant is about 65% of launched mass.

**Launch count, central:**
- Hardware: about 0.84 kt ÷ ~10.5 t average fill ≈ 80 Class M launches.
- Propellant: 1.57 kt ÷ 12 t ≈ 131 Class M launches.
- Total: about **210 Class M-equivalents over about 8 years, roughly 25 per year.**
- If Class H is available, this becomes about 27 super-heavy departures plus 80–160 tanker flights.

---

## 5. Technical Specifications

### 5.1 Payload classes

| Class | Max separated mass @ C3 −0.7 | Usable envelope | Interface | Qualified vehicles (planning) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S** | 0.6 t per port | ESPA-Grande volume | 24″ (610 mm) ESPA port | Any lunar or escape primary with ESPA ring |
| **M** | **12.0 t** (11.5 t design + 0.5 t margin) | Ø4.5 m × 10.0 m | 2624 mm clampband; 1575 mm alternate | Falcon Heavy (expendable centre), Vulcan VC6, New Glenn with kick stage, Starship expendable; Ariane 64 at ≤8.5 t derated |
| **H** | 80–100 t (6–8 Class M) | Ø8 m × 17 m | Multi-module adapter (MMA) carrying 6–8 Class M interfaces | Refuelled super-heavy |

**Class H rule:** no element may be designed to Class H alone. Every Class H manifest must be decomposable into Class M manifests at a known cost penalty.

**Launch vehicle capacity figures** (FH ~18–20 t, Vulcan VC6 ~12 t, Ariane 64 ~8.5 t at TLI-class C3) are planning assumptions. Vendor-confirmed numbers are an early 0A deliverable.

### 5.2 Design environment envelope (Class M, enveloping qualification)

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Quasi-static loads | +6.0 / −2.0 g axial; ±2.0 g lateral (combined; coupled loads analysis per vehicle) |
| Random vibration | 10.0 grms at acceptance; qualification at +3 dB / 2 min per axis |
| Acoustic | 142 dB OASPL at qualification |
| Separation shock | 2,000 g SRS (1–10 kHz) at the interface |
| Fundamental frequency | ≥ 10 Hz lateral, ≥ 25 Hz axial, stowed |
| Venting and thermal | Standard fairing depressurisation; ascent heat flux ≤ 1,135 W/m² at fairing jettison |

Starship's environment is not fully published. The MMA must attenuate it to this envelope.

### 5.3 Trajectory specification (SEL1 delivery)

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Injection energy | C3 = −0.6 to −0.8 km²/s². A lunar-flyby variant up to +2 is allowed for heliocentric-bound stages. |
| Transfer time | 90–120 days |
| Correction and insertion budget | Trajectory corrections 10–40 m/s; halo insertion 0–20 m/s. **EDC allocation 60 m/s.** |
| Station-keeping before capture | ≤ 5 m/s per year; parked passive units are captured within 180 days |
| Upper-stage disposal | Targeted to a heliocentric escape that does not return to the Earth–Moon system for ≥100 years, or to Earth reentry for reusable stages. No stage remains in cislunar space. Owned by bom-0-15; implemented here. |

### 5.4 Earth Departure Carrier (EDC)

The EDC is a cheap, series-produced, passive-at-arrival bus.

```
      +-------------------------------------------+
      |  EDC bus (Ø4.2 m ring, 1.6 m tall)        |
      |  - 2x I2 cartridges (5.3 t net each)      |  <-- cartridges are bom-0-16 hardware
      |  - green monoprop (AF-M315E/ASCENT) 60 m/s|
      |  - 1.5 kW array, 8 kWh battery            |
      |  - S-band TT&C, 2 LGA                     |
      |  - fiducials, retroreflectors, RF beacon  |
      |  - grapple fixture + 4x cartridge latches |
      +-------------------+-----------------------+
                          | 2624 mm clampband
                    [ launch vehicle ]
```

| Parameter | Specification |
|---|---|
| Dry mass | 550–700 t × 10⁻³ (i.e. 550–700 kg) |
| Monoprop load | ~340 kg at Isp 240 s for 60 m/s on 12 t |
| Payload (propellant variant) | 2 cartridges, 10.6 t net iodine, ~0.6 t cartridge shells (counted in tare) |
| Payload (cargo variant) | Pallet adapter for passive hardware up to 10.8 t |
| Payload efficiency | ~88% net iodine / separated mass |
| Thermal | Iodine cartridges held at 0–40 °C in cruise (vapour pressure 0.04 kPa at 25 °C) with sealed valves. No sublimation heating; heating is done by the tug at use. |
| Life | 1 year powered, then passivation (battery discharge, monoprop vented) |
| Lifetime quantity | ~130 propellant + ~40 cargo variants at the central case |
| Unit cost target | $3.5M (range $2.5–5M) at quantity ≥100 |

### 5.5 Cartridge interface (EDC ↔ tug)

This is owned jointly by bom-0-8, bom-0-16 and bom-0-4.

| Parameter | Specification |
|---|---|
| Cartridge geometry | Ø1.30 m × 1.25 m cylinder; 5.3 t net cast iodine (density ~4.5 effective, 4.93 theoretical) |
| Shell material | Titanium or Hastelloy-lined, because iodine attacks aluminium |
| Shell mass | ~300 kg each, including heaters, sublimator interface and latch |
| Mating | Four-point mechanical latch with heated dry-mate vapour coupling and a 28-pin power/data connector |
| Mate method | Tug-side manipulator or berthing. **No fluid or vapour transfer across a mated joint before the cartridge is latched and leak-checked.** |
| Leak rate | ≤ 1×10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s helium-equivalent per sealed cartridge (contamination requirement for co-manifest) |

### 6.1 Requirements

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| DEL-001 | Every hardware element shall be launchable as one or more Class M units on ≥2 independent launch vehicle families. |
| DEL-002 | No Phase 0 element shall remain in LEO for more than 14 days, except launch-vehicle operations. |
| DEL-003 | All upper stages shall be disposed per §5.3. Disposal success probability ≥ 0.999 per stage, consistent with a debris threshold tighter than 99%. |
| DEL-004 | P_LEO, P_dep, P_hand and P_site shall be reported separately in all cost products. |
| DEL-005 | Iodine cartridges shall not share a fairing with optics or unshielded arrays, except on Class H with an MMA barrier and verified leak rates. |
| DEL-006 | Loss of any single launch shall remove ≤1/3 of any critical function: plant throughput, site power, tug-fleet capacity, or node capture. |
| DEL-007 | The Earth-supply benchmark used at KDP-0B shall use the same price model and vintage as the bom-0-8 estimate. |
| DEL-008 | Passive delivered units shall survive ≥180 days parked in halo orbit, unattended, in safe mode. |

---

## 7. Autonomy, Control and Communication

**Intelligence lives in the tug and node, not the EDC.** The EDC is a cooperative passive target with a cheap bus. Proximity-operations autonomy (relative navigation, collision avoidance, capture) sits in bom-0-4 and bom-0-13 and is reused across about 170 captures. This keeps EDC cost near $3.5M.

**EDC autonomy:**
- On-board fault protection with sun-safe hold for ≥7 days without ground contact.
- Autonomous execution of uplinked correction burns.

## 8. Manufacturing and Launch-Site Operations

- **EDC series production.** About 170 units: one bus design and two payload variants (propellant, cargo). This is classic constellation-style manufacturing; build rate 2–3 per month at peak. Contract it as one firm-fixed-price production contract with a second source qualified at unit 20.

- **Cartridges** are bom-0-16 hardware. They are filled at the supplier and arrive sealed. Iodine (UN 3495, Class 8 corrosive with toxic subsidiary hazard) is far easier to handle at a launch site than hydrazine or xenon high-pressure loading:
  - No pad fuelling.
  - A ventilated cell with iodine vapour monitoring (exposure limit 0.1 ppm ceiling).
  - Scrubbers and spill kits.
  - Estimated $15–30M to build or lease.

- **Integration facility.** Leased commercial payload processing, Florida first, with a second site later. Throughput: 3 Class M units per month at peak.

- **Argon alternate (D-05).** High-pressure composite tanks give a tank fraction of 20–30% against about 6% for iodine. Gross propellant launched mass rises about 20%, adding roughly **$0.9–1.0B in the central case.** Argon also needs pad high-pressure loading or cryogenic handling. ## 9. Procurement and Manifest Strategy

1. **Block-buy delivery-to-C3 services**, not vehicles. Use indefinite-quantity contracts with ≥2 Class M vendors, with price indexed to a published launch-price index. **No vendor should carry more than 60% of hardware mass. Propellant may be concentrated.**

2. **Risk tiers:**
   - Tier 1 (unique or critical: plant modules, node, tug cores) flies only on vehicles with ≥10 consecutive successes.
   - Tier 2 (tugs beyond the first 4, spares) flies on any qualified vehicle.
   - Tier 3 (propellant) flies on early-flight or discounted vehicles. It is the programme's market shock absorber.

3. **Self-insurance.** At 1–3% failure rates over about 210 launches, expect 2–6 losses. Recommended bom-0-17 reserve: **5% of 8a + 8b launch value (~$0.45B central)**, plus 2 spare EDCs in rolling stock.

4. **Delivery sequence:**
   - Node first.
   - Then 4 tugs plus the first site cargo.
   - Then the remaining tugs interleaved with site cargo.
   - Then propellant as steady-state flow sized to demand.

**LEO is a pricing and integration boundary, not a mandatory warehouse.** Direct departure is preferable when it removes rendezvous, storage or assembly operations at acceptable cost.

### 3.2 Three delivery classes

| Class | Payloads | Preferred delivery method | Planning transit allowance² |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: scouts and pathfinders | Survey instruments, rendezvous scouts, demonstrators | Dedicated or rideshare launch with qualified chemical departure and onboard EP | 6–36 months |
| B: receiving infrastructure | SEL1 node, communications and servicing equipment | Chemical departure; onboard capture and stationkeeping | Weeks to several months |
| C: industrial equipment | Tugs, site power, robots, processing modules | Chemical departure followed by EP, or qualified self-delivery | 1–4 years |

²These are scheduling envelopes, not trajectory results. Poor targets may lie outside them and should fail the target gate.

### 3.3 Why not baseline EP spirals from LEO?

They can be mass-efficient but create unattractive early dependencies:

- Months of radiation-belt exposure;
- Large deployed arrays operating through crowded orbital regions;
- Repeated conjunction management;
- Long delays before productive departure;
- Charging, thermal and degradation exposure;
- Possible iodine contamination concerns;
- Dependence on immature MW-class propulsion before the industrial mission has begun.

**Recommendation:** Permit LEO-to-escape EP as an option demonstrated during 0A, but do not make it a critical-path assumption at programme start.

---

## 4. Mass architecture and campaign quantities

### 4.1 Phase 0A manifest

A useful reference allocation is:

| Cargo allocation | Reference mass |
|---|---:|
| Survey/scout flight hardware and hosted equipment | 4 t |
| Pathfinder hardware and associated power systems | 20 t |
| Delivery-relevant demonstrations, small receiving/servicing articles and flight spares | 8 t |
| Initial EP propellant | 10 t |
| Adapters, carriers, separation hardware and packaging allowances | 8 t |
| **Total** | **50 t** |

The **25–100 t** range reflects the difference between a compact pathfinder programme and a programme containing substantial power/propulsion demonstration hardware. bom-0-8 does not prescribe the pathfinder design or charge for its manufacture.

### 4.2 Conditional Phase 0B reference manifest

| Cargo allocation | Reference mass |
|---|---:|
| Twelve cargo tugs, approximately 65 t dry each | 780 t |
| NEA site power, storage and thermal equipment | 550 t |
| Beneficiation and primary processing hardware | 300 t |
| Mining and handling robots | 160 t |
| SEL1 receiving-node hardware | 200 t |
| Surface logistics, communications and miscellaneous installed equipment | 130 t |
| Delivered spares and replacement hardware | 280 t |
| **Allocated dry hardware** | **2,400 t** |
| Hardware mass-growth allowance, 15% | 360 t |
| Initial EP propellant inventory | 800 t |
| Delivery-only carriers, adapters, cradles and transport equipment | 440 t |
| **Total programme cargo manifest** | **4,000 t** |

These numbers are **transport-sizing placeholders** for other BOM owners to replace. In particular, the 65 t tug assumption must include its own arrays, radiators, thrusters, tanks and structure, avoiding duplication with site power.

The delivered mass is less than 4,000 t because:

- Some initial propellant is consumed during commissioning and delivery;
- Delivery-only hardware may be disposed of or retained outside the operating sites;
- Some equipment is accepted at SEL1, some at the NEA.

For illustration, consuming 400 t of EP propellant and disposing of all 440 t of delivery equipment leaves approximately **3,160 t at operating locations**, comprising installed hardware, growth allowance and retained propellant. The actual destination-by-destination mass balance must replace this illustration after trajectory design.

### 4.3 Launch count

Launch count cannot be obtained by dividing the manifest by a vehicle’s advertised LEO capacity.

For a reference mixed campaign:

- Approximately **55%** of cargo could use LEO staging or low-energy handover;
- Approximately **45%** could use direct higher-energy departure;
- Illustrative programme-cargo capacity is **80 t per LEO mission** and **25 t per direct-departure mission**.

That gives approximately:

\[
N \approx \frac{2{,}200}{80}+\frac{1{,}800}{25}\approx100
\]

launch missions.

These capacities are assumptions requiring provider confirmation. Additional departure-stage or propellant launches may be needed in an aggregated architecture.

**Planning range:** approximately **60–160 principal launch missions** for the reference-scale industrial campaign, with a potentially wider range if the programme selects a substantially different launch architecture.

This is a major logistics campaign, not a handful of heavy-lift flights.

---

## 5. Transportation performance and technical requirements

### 5.1 Earth departure

For a circular 200 km parking orbit, impulsive departure requirements are approximately:

| Departure condition | Approximate departure burn |
|---|---:|
| Near-escape, \(C_3=0\) km²/s² | 3.2 km/s |
| \(C_3=10\) km²/s² | 3.6 km/s |
| \(C_3=15\) km²/s² | 3.9 km/s |

These follow the standard two-body relation:

\[
\Delta v =
\sqrt{\frac{2\mu_E}{r}+C_3}
-\sqrt{\frac{\mu_E}{r}}
\]

They exclude gravity losses, steering losses, reserves and finite-burn effects.

At 450 s specific impulse, a 3.2–3.9 km/s burn consumes approximately **52–59% of the pre-burn ideal stage-plus-payload mass**, before accounting for stage dry mass. Consequently, an advertised LEO payload must never be represented as an equal-mass NEA delivery capability.

**Procurement requirement:** providers shall supply payload-versus-\(C_3\) curves and trajectory-specific separation states, not merely “deep-space capable” marketing descriptions.

### 5.2 Electric transport screening

For a representative 1.5 MWe tug:

\[
T=\frac{2\eta P}{v_e}
\]

Using \(\eta=0.62\), \(P=1.5\) MW and \(v_e=30\) km/s:

- Thrust: **62 N**;
- Propellant flow: **2.07 g/s**;
- Full-power annual consumption: **65 t/year**;
- Consumption at 60% annual thrust duty: **39 t/year**.

Twelve such vehicles consume approximately **470 t/year** at that operating point.

For a 350 t vehicle-plus-load, initial acceleration is approximately:

\[
a=1.8\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}
\]

or about **15 m/s per thrusting day**. This supports months-to-years trajectory planning, not chemical-stage scheduling.

For an illustrative **6–10 km/s** EP manoeuvre requirement and exhaust velocity of **25–35 km/s**, ideal propellant fractions are approximately **16–33%**. Actual requirements depend strongly on target, power availability, throttling, departure energy and return strategy.

### 5.3 Replenishment is separate from initial deployment

The initial 800 t propellant allowance is **not** a lifetime supply.

A provisional steady-state delivery allowance is:

- **300–900 t/year of EP propellant**;
- Plus spares and replacement equipment;
- Potentially **$0.5–2.5B/year in Earth-origin transport**, depending on packaging and destination.

This annual transport is not included indefinitely in the one-time 0B deployment estimate. Before KDP-0B, the programme must define the funded operating horizon and carry that recurring logistics obligation in its lifecycle budget.

---

## 6. Payload envelopes, interfaces and subsystems

### 6.1 Transport module classes

| Attribute | Standard module | Heavy module |
|---|---:|---:|
| Nominal transported mass | 10–25 t | 25–60 t |
| Preferred stowed diameter | ≤4.5 m | ≤7 m, provider-dependent |
| Preferred stowed length | ≤8 m | ≤12 m |
| Transport electrical service | 0.5–5 kW typical | 2–15 kW typical |
| Peak checkout allowance | Up to 15 kW | Up to 30 kW |
| Unpowered survival | 72 hours minimum target | 72 hours minimum target |

These are **design-to envelopes**, not promises of compatibility with every launcher. Fairing dynamic envelopes, centre-of-mass limits and adapter loads govern final compatibility.

Large arrays and radiators must launch stowed. Their deployed dimensions belong to their equipment specifications; bom-0-8 owns clearance and deployment compatibility during transport.

### 6.2 Subsystems

**Mechanical accommodation**

- Standard load-transfer and lifting interfaces;
- Replaceable adapter rings or bolted frames;
- Accessible lifting points with propellant-loaded and dry configurations documented;
- Transport restraints protecting bearings, deployables and precision surfaces;
- Verified centre of mass and inertia tensor.

**Separation and deployment**

- Low-shock separation where warranted;
- Independent separation confirmation;
- Positive clearance before deployment or thruster activation;
- No untracked released caps, straps or fragments;
- Deployment inhibits independent of ground commands.

**Electrical accommodation**

- Prefer **100–150 V DC** housekeeping distribution during carriage;
- Galvanic isolation between carrier and payload;
- Defined bonding, grounding and fault-current paths;
- Site 1–3 kV robot distribution must not be energised through an unqualified launch interface.

**Thermal accommodation**

- Temperature limits supplied by each payload owner;
- Survival heaters sized for launch delay, coast and failed handover cases;
- No assumption that a dormant multi-year payload survives passively;
- Transport power and thermal models include eclipse, attitude and array nondeployment cases.

**Fluid and propellant accommodation**

- Commodity-specific tanks, valves and cleanliness requirements;
- No common iodine/argon transfer system assumed;
- Loading on Earth is preferred for early flights;
- Orbital transfer introduced only where it has passed relevant-environment qualification and improves the lifecycle case.

**Navigation aids**

- Optical fiducials, retroreflectors where useful, passive safe-hold geometry;
- Independent cooperative navigation aids for large capture operations;
- No dependence on uninterrupted ground contact for collision avoidance.

### 6.3 Propellant-specific constraints

**Iodine reference case**

- Solid storage can simplify volume requirements, but does not eliminate tankage, thermal-control or compatibility problems.
- Sublimation, heated feed lines, seals, corrosion, contamination and long-duration isolation require testing.
- Transport packaging must limit contamination of arrays, optics, radiators and processing equipment.

**Argon alternate**

- High-pressure storage can create substantial tank mass and volume penalties.
- An initial trade should examine approximately **20–35 MPa** storage, with actual pressure established from qualified vessels and system optimisation.
- Cryogenic argon may be investigated, but is not the baseline: it introduces boil-off, refrigeration and storage-duration dependencies.

Neither option is sufficiently defined to freeze the delivery mass fraction today.

---

## 7. Autonomy, control and communications

### 7.1 Required autonomy

Delivery vehicles and payloads shall support:

- Autonomous safe mode and power-positive attitude;
- Fault isolation and restart without immediate ground intervention;
- Autonomous burn interruption on propulsion or attitude faults;
- Keep-out-zone enforcement;
- Collision avoidance and retreat during rendezvous;
- Autonomous protection against battery depletion and thermal excursions;
- Recovery from communication outages lasting at least **72 hours** in normal cruise configurations.

For close approach, ground operators may authorise phases, but onboard control must execute safety-critical responses.

### 7.2 Navigation and capture

Preliminary design targets, subject to receiving-interface design:

- Terminal docking/capture relative velocity: **≤0.05–0.10 m/s**;
- Metre-class relative navigation before final approach;
- Decimetre-class relative navigation for the final capture phase where required;
- Independent abort manoeuvre capability;
- Passive collision-safe trajectories wherever orbital geometry permits.

These are not asteroid landing requirements. NEA surface installation and anchoring remain separate, jointly controlled activities with bom-0-2/3.

### 7.3 Communications interface

Transport does not justify a new bulk-data network.

Allocate:

- Routine health and navigation: **1–20 kbps per active vehicle**;
- Encounter/deployment engineering telemetry: **0.1–2 Mbps**, when link geometry supports it;
- High-rate image playback by schedule, not continuous streaming.

Use store-and-forward operation and interoperable space-link protocols. DSN or commercial ground access must be purchased and budgeted through bom-0-9/10.

---

## 8. Manufacturing, integration and acceptance

### 8.1 Manufacturing approach

Build **three families of transport accommodations**, not a unique carrier for every payload:

1. Scout/pathfinder adapters;
2. Standard industrial cargo cradles;
3. Heavy power/tug module accommodations.

Use metallic primary structures and conventional joining where they offer inspectability and repairability. Exotic mass reduction is justified only by demonstrated net delivered-cost savings.

Manufacture early interface simulators so equipment teams can verify:

- Fit and access;
- Harness routing;
- Separation clearance;
- Ground-handling loads;
- Connector mating;
- Thermal and electrical compatibility.

### 8.2 Qualification strategy

Each payload must have an approved combination of qualification testing, analysis and similarity justification covering:

- Quasi-static and coupled dynamic loads;
- Acoustic and vibration environments;
- Separation shock;
- Electromagnetic compatibility;
- Thermal-vacuum survival;
- Battery and pressure-system safety;
- Propellant compatibility;
- Long-duration dormant operation;
- Deployable release and restraint ageing.

Do not invent generic acceleration limits and treat them as launcher requirements. Preliminary sizing may examine **3–6 g axial** environments, but contracted vehicle environments and coupled-loads analysis govern acceptance.

### 8.3 Delivery acceptance

Use four distinct milestones:

1. **Launch acceptance:** correct payload separation and injected state.
2. **Cruise acceptance:** power, communications, thermal control and propulsion operational.
3. **Destination acceptance:** agreed arrival state or safe rendezvous achieved.
4. **Operational handover:** installation interface, deployment and checkout complete to the agreed boundary.

Contracts should not pay the entire “delivered” price at launch.

---

## 9. Development roadmap and readiness gates

### Phase 0A-1 — Architecture and supplier competition

Indicative duration: **12–18 months**.

- Establish the configuration-controlled cargo register;
- Obtain trajectory-specific launch and delivery proposals;
- Complete target-dependent mass and energy models;
- Identify propellant storage and transport hazards;
- Freeze provisional interface standards;
- Identify technologies that could end the programme if they fail.

### Phase 0A-2 — Relevant subsystem demonstrations

Indicative duration: **18–36 months**, partly overlapping.

Demonstrate:

- Long-duration dormant payload survival;
- Representative separation and deployment;
- Propellant/material compatibility;
- Power/propulsion interfaces;
- Rendezvous and capture;
- Autonomous transport fault protection.

Internal milestones target **TRL 4–5**, consistent with D-02.

### Phase 0A-3 — End-to-end pathfinder delivery

Indicative duration: **2–5 years**, driven by destination and trajectory.

Deliver an operationally meaningful payload, not merely a ballast article, and demonstrate the transport architecture’s critical interfaces.

A small EP flight does **not** by itself qualify a MW-class tug. Relevant scaling must cover power processing, thermal rejection, lifetime, plume interaction, fault response and system integration.

### KDP-0B — Mandatory closure

No irreversible industrial campaign commitment until:

- Target orbit and physical properties support the delivery plan;
- Signed Phase 1 demand fixes product, quality, quantity and delivery dates;
- All project-ending technologies reach **TRL 6 in a relevant environment, without waivers**;
- Launch and transport capacity is contractible;
- Propellant supply and packaging are credible;
- Lifecycle economics include replenishment and replacement;
- Licence, liability and contamination requirements are satisfied;
- Earth-supplied material remains a costed fallback.

### Phase 0B — Staged industrial deployment

Sequence:

1. Receiving and navigation infrastructure;
2. Initial NEA power and communications;
3. First processing train and robot set;
4. First qualified production-transport tranche;
5. Expansion only after commissioning and acceptance.

Hold later tranches where possible until preceding equipment demonstrates performance.

---

## 10. Cost estimate and accounting method

### 10.1 Keep LEO and delivered prices separate

Use:

\[
C_{\text{bom-0-8}}
=
C_{\text{LEO access}}
+
C_{\text{onward delivery}}
+
C_{\text{campaign integration}}
\]

For direct-injection contracts, these are **accounting allocations within one purchased service**, not three separately purchased flights. Obtain a provider LEO-reference quote and the incremental price for the actual departure condition; do not add a full direct-launch price to a full LEO-launch price.

### 10.2 Phase 0B scenarios

| Scenario | Cargo manifest | LEO-reference access | Onward delivery | Campaign integration | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Low | 2,500 t | $2.00B at $800/kg | $1.00B | $0.25B | **$3.25B** |
| Reference | 4,000 t | $4.80B at $1,200/kg | $2.00B | $0.50B | **$7.30B** |
| High | 6,000 t | $10.80B at $1,800/kg | $4.00B | $0.90B | **$15.70B** |

Onward delivery covers purchased departure stages, carrier services, delivery-only equipment and the transport-service portion of using programme tugs. It does **not** repurchase tug hardware or EP propellant commodity.

The low case requires favourable launch pricing, manageable departure energy, relatively light hardware and little redesign. The high case represents a larger, less efficient campaign—not a probabilistic confidence bound.

### 10.3 Phase 0A allowance

| Element | Range |
|---|---:|
| Launch services | $100–350M |
| Departure and onward delivery | $80–350M |
| Mission-specific integration and campaigns | $70–200M |
| **Total** | **$250–900M** |

Early demonstrations are disproportionately expensive per kilogram because they buy dedicated opportunities, schedule assurance and mission-specific integration.

### 10.4 Effective delivered price

At the reference point:

- Cargo-reference cost: \( \$7.3B / 4{,}000t \approx \$1{,}825/kg \);
- If approximately 3,160 t remains at accepted destinations: approximately **$2,310/kg**;
- If counting only the 2,760 t installed-hardware allocation, including growth allowance: approximately **$2,645/kg**.

These are different denominators and must not be interchanged. None is a price per kilogram of asteroid product.

### 10.5 Position on the round-2 proposals

**Mass:** The proposed **2.5–6 kt industrial range** is a reasonable working envelope. The narrower 2.5–3.5 kt range is not yet justified given tug, radiator, propellant and packaging uncertainty. An 8 kt case should remain a stress case, not silently become the baseline.

**Cost:** A **$3–6B total** is possible only toward the favourable end of mass and service pricing. It is too narrow for current planning. A broader approximately **$3.5–16.6B for 0A plus 0B**, with a **$7.8B reference point**, better exposes the unresolved decisions.

**Unit price:** The round-2 **$3,000–12,000/kg** range may describe small dedicated deep-space missions or an adverse campaign, but is not useful as a single multiplier without a destination and mass boundary. My reference estimate is lower because it assumes industrial procurement and use of programme-owned transport assets. Those assumptions require validation during 0A.

---

## 11. Principal risks and mitigations

| Risk | Consequence | Required response |
|---|---|---|
| Target selected for ore quality but not accessibility | Delivery architecture becomes uneconomic | Joint geology–trajectory–operations target gate |
| MW EP fails lifetime or scaling tests | Fleet cannot deploy or replenish | No-waiver TRL 6 gate; retain chemical departure options |
| Iodine incompatibility or contamination | Payload and propulsion degradation | Material/plume tests; preserve argon alternate |
| Launch provider concentration | Cost growth or prolonged stand-down | Dual-source interfaces and staged procurement |
| Mass growth | Additional launch lots and delayed commissioning | Configuration-controlled mass register with transported growth allowance |
| Multi-year transit failures | Equipment arrives degraded | Dormancy qualification, checkout capability and replaceable modules |
| Assembly complexity | Campaign bottleneck and collision exposure | Minimise mandatory assembly; demonstrate critical operations in 0A |
| Propellant tankage underestimated | Manifest and costs fail to close | Tank-level mass/volume models before architecture freeze |
| Receiving node not ready | Cargo stranded or forced into unsafe loiter | Destination-readiness release criteria |
| Launch cadence unavailable | Deployment spans excessive years | Contract cadence and integration capacity, not merely launch price |
| Liability/licensing delay | Launch or disposal blocked | Early regulator engagement and controlled disposal plans |

### Debris and contamination

bom-0-8 must implement the requirements owned by bom-0-15:

- No intentional release of untracked hardware;
- Passivation of spent delivery stages;
- Controlled disposition or approved stable disposal;
- Collision-risk assessment throughout Earth departure;
- Propellant containment and plume management;
- Prevention of contamination that compromises target science or processing.

D-03 remains interim. **I would not invent a numerical “acceptable loss” threshold for this proposal.** Demonstrate ALARP, model credible breakup and contamination cases, and establish the quantitative ceiling with the licensing state before the relevant flight commitment.

---

## 12. Open engineering questions

The following must be answered before a firm 0B launch budget is credible:

1. **Which NEA, which arrival windows, and what delivered-state requirement?**
2. **What exact Fe-Ni material, purity, quantity and date does Phase 1 contract to receive?**
3. **What is each tug’s fully burdened dry mass**, including arrays, radiators, tanks, shielding and reserves?
4. **Can the selected EP system demonstrate MW-scale relevant-environment performance and life?**
5. **What is the storage and packaging mass of iodine versus argon?**
6. **How much propellant must be carried during initial deployment versus replenished later?**
7. **Which modules genuinely require orbital assembly?**
8. **What launch rate can providers and the programme’s integration facilities sustain?**
9. **Can SEL1 receiving infrastructure be ready before the first cargo arrivals?**
10. **Which obligations continue during multi-year cruise, and who pays for them?**
11. **What replacement strategy follows a failed industrial-module delivery?**
12. **When does direct Earth supply outperform asteroid-derived material for the signed Phase 1 demand?**

## Final recommendation

Approve a **$250–900M staged 0A launch-and-delivery allowance**, with **$500M as the reference planning allocation**, and require 0A to replace assumptions with supplier quotations, target-specific trajectories and demonstrated interfaces.

Carry **2.5–6 kt and $3.25–15.7B** as the conditional 0B deployment envelope, with **4 kt and $7.3B** as a transparent reference case—not an authorised commitment.

The decisive engineering product of 0A should be a **closed delivery ledger**: every module has a mass, launch opportunity, departure state, propulsion allocation, arrival condition, acceptance test, disposal plan and accountable price. Until that ledger closes, industrial throughput and launch affordability remain hypotheses.

---

# bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery: Consensus Synthesis

## Key Specifications

- **No LEO electric-propulsion spiral in the baseline.** All three models want chemical departure on commercial vehicles to high energy or escape (C3 ≈ 0, or SEL1 transfer at C3 ≈ −0.7 km²/s²).
  - All three cite Van Allen belt degradation of MW-class arrays and debris exposure.
  - GPT alone keeps LEO-to-escape EP as a 0A-demonstrated option. Claude rejects it outright for tugs.
- **Commercial launch only, with interfaces that allow at least two vendors.** No bespoke launcher or kick-stage development.
  - All three treat super-heavy vehicles as useful, but warn against a single-vendor design dependency.
  - This warning is weakest in Gemini, whose 0B plan depends on super-heavy vehicles.
- **LEO and delivered prices are reported separately.** No model accepts a single undifferentiated $/kg figure.
  - Claude: four prices (P_LEO, P_dep, P_hand, P_site), defined in §1.3.
  - GPT: LEO access, onward delivery and campaign integration as three cost terms.
  - Gemini: "LEO-equivalent" mass and price alongside "delivered" mass and price.
  - GPT warns that, for direct-injection contracts, these are accounting allocations within one purchased service, not separate flights.
- **Phase 0A launches tens of tonnes, at roughly $0.2–0.9B.**

  | Model | 0A mass | 0A cost range | Reference value |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Claude | ~16 t (7–34 t) | $0.25–0.74B | $0.42B |
  | Gemini | 50–80 t delivered | $0.20–0.48B | — |
  | GPT | 50 t (25–100 t) | $0.25–0.90B | $0.50B |

  All three expect early per-kg prices to be high because 0A buys dedicated or rideshare missions.
- **Phase 0B launched mass is of order 2.4–4 kt** at the planning point. This is several hundred tonnes of hardware plus a propellant block of comparable or larger size.

  | Model | Central / reference | Range |
  |---|---|---|
  | Claude | 2.43 kt | 1.3–4.5 kt (P10–P90) |
  | Gemini | ~2.4 kt delivered | ~3.05–3.5 kt LEO-equivalent |
  | GPT | 4.0 kt cargo manifest | 2.5–6 kt |

  - All three reject 8 kt as a planning value. GPT keeps it only as a stress case.
- **EP propellant launches from Earth in sealed, Earth-filled containers.**
  - Claude: iodine cartridges, 5.3 t net each, carried two per Earth Departure Carrier (EDC).
  - Gemini: "smart tanks".
  - GPT: commodity-specific tanks, with Earth loading preferred.
  - No model baselines in-space fluid transfer or a cryogenic depot.
  - Iodine is costed as the reference propellant and argon as the alternate (D-05). All three flag argon's high-pressure tank mass penalty: Claude puts its tank fraction at 20–30%; GPT proposes a 20–35 MPa trade study.
- **Upper stages are disposed of under contract.** Options are heliocentric escape or Earth re-entry. Nothing is left in LEO, high Earth orbit or cislunar space.
  - bom-0-8 implements the bom-0-15 policy and pays for the disposal burns.
  - Claude sets a disposal success probability of ≥0.999 per stage. GPT declines to set a numeric threshold until D-03 is resolved.
- **Launch environment design envelope**, subject to vehicle-specific coupled loads analysis:
  - Acoustic about 142 dB OASPL (Claude, Gemini).
  - Axial load of about 6 g (Claude +6/−2 g; Gemini ~6 g; GPT 3–6 g preliminary).
  - Scouts fly on ESPA-Grande rideshare ports (Claude, Gemini); GPT allows rideshare or dedicated launch.
  - Large modules use 2624 mm clampbands (Claude, Gemini).
  - Providers must supply payload-versus-C3 curves, not LEO capacity figures (explicit in GPT and Claude).
- **0B is a large logistics campaign, released in tranches only after KDP-0B.**
  - The campaign spans tens to hundreds of launches.
  - Sequence: receiving node and infrastructure first, then the first tugs and site cargo, then expansion only after commissioning.
  - Hardware is modular, so a single launch failure is survivable. Claude sets this as requirement DEL-006: losing one launch removes ≤1/3 of any critical function.

## Divergent Views

- **0B cost and what it includes**: Claude recommends a $9.3B P50 planning value (P10–P90 $4–16B). This covers propellant for the full 5-year production run (1.57 kt gross) plus about 170 EDCs and pallets.
  - Gemini prefers $2.5–5.4B. Its total is $2.7–5.9B including 0A. This assumes mature reusable super-heavy pricing and covers only 1.2 kt of *initial* propellant.
  - GPT suggests $7.3B as a reference (range $3.25–15.7B). This covers only 800 t of initial propellant. Recurring replenishment of 300–900 t/yr, about $0.5–2.5B/yr, is excluded and must be added at the gate.
  - **These totals are not like-for-like.** Once GPT's replenishment is added over a 4–6 year run, its figure converges toward or above Claude's.
- **Mass floor and scaling basis**: Claude recommends 1.3–4.5 kt. It rejects the round-2 floor of 2.5 kt because D-01 sizes 0B by signed demand, and a low-demand case (0.6 kt/yr × 4 yr) needs only about 1.3 kt.
  - Gemini prefers about 2.4 kt delivered. Its plant (800 t) and tugs (15 × 50 t) are heavier than Claude's. Its figures are internally inconsistent: it states escape payload is 30–35% of LEO capacity, but its ~3.5 kt "LEO-equivalent" total implies a far higher ratio.
  - GPT suggests 2.5–6 kt with a 4 kt reference. This uses heavier placeholders: tugs at 65 t dry each, 550 t of site power, and 440 t of delivery-only carriers.
- **Handover point and the deep-space leg**: Claude recommends one gateway at SEL1, reached by direct injection at C3 ≈ −0.7. Passive EDCs and pallets are captured by the receiving node (bom-0-13). Tugs carry site cargo on outbound legs that would otherwise fly empty, so the NEA leg is a marginal cost.
  - Gemini prefers handover in high Earth orbit or at escape. Tugs take over for transit to the NEA or SEL1, and smart tanks dock with tugs in high Earth orbit.
  - GPT suggests a mixed campaign. About 55% of cargo uses LEO staging or low-energy handover, and about 45% departs directly. Acceptance has four milestones (launch, cruise, destination, operational handover), and the "delivered" price is not paid in full at launch.
- **Module size, launcher dependence and tug power**: Claude recommends a "Class M" module limit of ≤12 t at C3 −0.7 within Ø4.5 m × 10 m, flyable on at least two vehicle families.
  - On that basis Claude recommends tugs of 1.2–1.5 MWe launched as two modules each. 2.5 MWe tugs would be infeasible without demonstrated refuelled super-heavy delivery.
  - Gemini prefers designing to fairings up to 8 m × 18 m, launched as 20–30 super-heavy flights.
  - GPT suggests two classes: standard (10–25 t, ≤4.5 m) and heavy (25–60 t, ≤7 m), with a 1.5 MWe tug used for screening.
- **Launch price basis**: Claude recommends departure prices (P_dep) of about $3.8k/kg for hardware and $3.0k/kg for propellant, and SEL1 handover prices (P_hand) of $4.7k/kg for hardware and $3.8k/kg for iodine. It treats mature super-heavy pricing as an upside, not a planning value.
  - Gemini prefers $4–6k/kg delivered in 0A, falling to $2.5–4.5k/kg in 0B.
  - GPT suggests $800–1,800/kg to LEO plus an onward-delivery charge, giving about $1.8–2.6k/kg effective at the reference point.
  - All three regard the round-2 $3,000–12,000/kg range as ambiguous: it does not say which boundary it refers to.
- **Cadence and launch count**: Claude recommends about 210 Class M-equivalent launches over about 8 years, roughly 25 per year. The alternative is about 27 super-heavy departures plus 80–160 tanker flights.
  - Gemini prefers 20–30 super-heavy launches within a 24-month campaign.
  - GPT suggests 60–160 principal missions, with additional departure-stage or tanker flights if the architecture aggregates in orbit.

## Open Questions

1. **Tug fully burdened dry mass and module split** (bom-0-4). Estimates range from Claude's ~24 t to GPT's ~65 t. Can a 1.2–1.5 MWe tug fit two ≤12 t modules? Should the Class M limit be 12 t or 15 t, given vendor-confirmed C3 −0.7 performance?
2. **Propellant intensity, horizon and packaging.**
   - Intensity: Claude estimates 0.15–0.35 kg of iodine per kg of product.
   - Horizon: what share is initial load versus replenishment over the funded operating period?
   - Packaging: iodine versus argon tank fraction. Claude estimates argon adds about 20% launched mass and $0.9–1.0B.
   - Ownership: should propellant launch sit in bom-0-8 (8b) or bom-0-16?
3. **In-space propellant handling at TRL 6.** This means cartridge or tank mating, heated vapour coupling, long-term sealed iodine storage, and autonomous capture of passive targets in halo orbit. Can the 0A pathfinder (bom-0-12) fly these before KDP-0B, as D-02 requires with no waivers?
4. **Is a LEO propellant route worth adding?** This would be a LEO depot plus a dedicated cislunar EP shuttle (Claude's Mode P, estimated to save $1–2B) or GPT's partial LEO staging. The saving must be weighed against debris and radiation-belt exposure under ALARP (D-03).
5. **Launch-rate capacity.** Can providers, ranges and integration facilities sustain 25 or more high-energy launches per year? What are the FAA licensing and environmental limits on that cadence?
6. **Earth-supply benchmark and gateway location.**
   - Claude estimates the launch cost embedded in each kg of product at about 30–45% of the Earth-supply benchmark price at any launch price. On this view, cheaper launch weakens 0B's relative economics.
   - Which launch-price index, and which vintage, should govern KDP-0B?
   - Moving the gateway to SEL4/L5 would add roughly +1 to +3 km²/s² of C3 and 1–2 years of latency (D-04).

## Recommended Approach

1. **Replace the single line total with a mass × price ledger split into three sub-lines**: 8a hardware delivery, 8b propellant delivery, 8c delivery infrastructure.
   - Report P_LEO, P_dep, P_hand and P_site separately, and never add P_site to the tug or propellant lines.
   - Restate the round-2 $3,000–12,000/kg against these boundaries.
   - The end product of 0A should be GPT's "closed delivery ledger": every module has a mass, launch slot, departure state, propulsion allocation, arrival condition, acceptance test, disposal plan and price.
2. **Fund 0A at about $0.45B reference, within a $0.25–0.9B staged envelope.**
   - Cover scout rideshares, pathfinder launches and subsystem demonstrations.
   - Develop the carrier (EDC) to critical design review.
   - Obtain binding, C3-specific vendor quotes by 2027.
3. **Carry 0B as a planning value only, of about $8–9B P50 within a $3–16B band.** Re-size it at KDP-0B from signed demand.
   - Reject the 2.5 kt mass floor. Plan on about 1.3–6 kt, with a central value near 2.5–4 kt.
   - Gemini's $3–6B is treated as an upside requiring mature refuelled super-heavy delivery, not a baseline.
   - Include propellant replenishment over the full funded 0B run, not only the initial load.
4. **Baseline direct high-energy injection to an SEL1 handover, consistent with D-04.**
   - Prohibit LEO loiter of more than 14 days for Phase 0 elements.
   - Use outbound tug legs for site cargo.
   - Keep a LEO propellant route as a funded study, to be decided by 2030.
   - Contractually require upper-stage disposal to heliocentric escape or re-entry.
5. **Design every element to a dual-sourced module class of about 12 t at C3 −0.7 within Ø4.5 m.**
   - A super-heavy class (multi-module bundles) is used only for bundling, and every bundle must decompose into standard modules.
   - Direct bom-0-4 to close the two-module tug trade (1.2–1.5 MWe versus up to 2.5 MWe) by 2028.
   - Apply DEL-006: any single launch loss removes ≤1/3 of any critical function.
6. **Manage risk through tiering and self-insurance, not commercial insurance.**
   - Fly unique critical hardware on mature vehicles. Fly fungible propellant on discounted or early-flight vehicles.
   - Hold a launch-loss reserve in bom-0-17 of about 5% of launch value (~$0.45B central).
   - Buffer at least one year of propellant at the receiving node.
   - Pay for delivery against GPT's staged acceptance milestones, not in full at launch.
7. **Make the 0A pathfinder carry the delivery-critical demonstrations to TRL 6.** These are cartridge or tank exchange, halo-orbit capture, and dormant-payload survival.
   - Require the KDP-0B economic gate to use the same launch price model and vintage for both Phase 0 costs and the Earth-supplied-material benchmark (Claude's DEL-007).
   - The aim is that the capability framing of D-01 is assessed honestly.
